# Design Taste: complete single-file edition
<!-- Generated by scripts/sync-skill.sh. SKILL body, then every reference file. -->


# Design Taste — Anthony's Prescription

This skill is a ruleset distilled from 87 rounds of side-by-side comparisons covering 108 design dimensions, extended in v2 with defaults for surfaces those rounds never reached (interactive UI, decks, critique, localization, brand files), drawn from an analysis of the open-source Open Design project and filtered through his rules. It tells you how Anthony would design something himself. It does not prescribe pixel sizes, hex codes, or durations; it prescribes relationships, so it works at any size, aspect ratio, format, tool, or brand. It names no agent product and works the same in any harness.

## How the files fit

Read this file fully, then open `references/index.md` and load only what the task touches. Everything is one level deep.

- `references/principles/<category>.md` — **validated rules**, one file per category (composition, typography, color, motion, …), each tagged with its layer and the rounds that produced it. Read the categories relevant to the task before designing.
- `references/evidence.md` — the coverage tracker and round log (his picks and reasoning). For resolving ambiguity and quoting him.
- Imported references (rules tagged `OD`; defaults where no validated rule exists): `process-and-critique.md`, `ui-craft.md`, `formats.md`, `media-prompts.md`, `scripts-and-direction.md`, `brand-and-registers.md`, `open-design-crosswalk.md`. `index.md` says when to read each.

**Two tiers.** Validated rules (this file + `principles/`) always win. Imported `OD` rules fill gaps, never override a validated rule, dealbreaker or non-negotiable, and cannot by themselves justify a BLOCK in a critique.

## Layers (how rules combine)

- **L1 — Foundation.** True in every piece. Never trade these away for style.
- **L2 — Tonal presets.** Dials that move with the concept (quiet/premium, playful, energetic, luxury, warm/inviting, plus the product, broadsheet, paper, showcase and instrument registers below).
- **L3 — Brand constraints.** A client's guidelines override L1 and L2 *preferences*. They never override the **non-negotiables** below; when a brand rule breaks one, change the minimum needed and flag the conflict to the user. Procedure for brand files: `references/brand-and-registers.md`.

## Core tenets (read first, always)

0. **Concept drives execution. Always. But the design principles still hold.** Read the subject, audience, channel and imagery first; let them choose type, palette temperature, motion energy, crop and camera. The foundation never bends.
1. **Everything must read as intentional.** Anything that could be mistaken for an accident or a default is wrong. Deviate decisively or not at all — a small offset, a slight angle, a one-sided bleed, a near-match color all read as errors.
2. **Hierarchy is enforced and follows meaning.** The reader never wonders what comes first. Spatial order, size, weight, color and motion order all follow the reading order and the meaning.
3. **Restraint over effect.** Drama lives in one place (the image or the headline); everything else is calm. No gratuitous bold, bounce, shadow, glow, ornament, or lone accent.
4. **Legibility is non-negotiable.** Contrast, reading time, no collisions, no near-tangents.
5. **Decide by the concept and the real assets.** Crops, camera moves, tints, dark modes and palettes come from this subject and this photograph.

## Non-negotiables (survive any brand override)

1. Accessible text contrast against whatever is actually behind the text (check images, gradients, opacity).
2. In motion, every frame holds long enough to read **all** of its text before anything exits.
3. Text links in UI are colored **and** underlined at rest.
4. No glyph collisions between lines; no near-tangents (elements almost touching, especially corner-to-corner — including text against features in a photo).
5. Reading order and enforced hierarchy.

## Workflow

1. **Read the brief.** Identify subject, audience, channel (glance media vs. poster vs. reference media), format/aspect ratio, whether there's motion or sound, script and language, and whether brand guidelines exist. If brand guidelines exist, load them as L3. Ask the user only for what would change the direction, structure or format; if you cannot ask, proceed on the most defensible reading and list your assumptions in the delivery note (`process-and-critique.md`).
2. **Pick the register from the concept** (presets below). Do not apply a default house style to every brief, and do not hand the user a style menu: choosing is the job.
3. **State the system in one sentence** before building a non-trivial piece: register and why, ground, type roles, accent logic, motion character. It lets the user redirect cheaply.
4. **Build the structure (L1)** — image-first, top-down reading chain, strict grid, golden-section proportions, one unbroken text block. See *Composition*, *Grid*, *Text/Image* in `principles/`. For an interface, also read `ui-craft.md`; for a specific deliverable (deck, dashboard, email, …), `formats.md`.
5. **Set the voice (L2)** — typeface, palette, motion character from the preset; pull colors from the actual imagery.
6. **Pre-flight check** — run the checklist below, plus the self-review loop in `process-and-critique.md`. Fix everything before showing work. If you can render the result, look at it at the real format(s) and measure rather than trust arithmetic. Then say briefly what you checked and anything you had to compromise; never claim a check you did not run.
7. **When critiquing**, use the scored format in `process-and-critique.md`: cite the specific principle (and its category) a design violates, separate must-fixes from quick wins, and propose the concrete fix.

## Structural defaults (L1, every register)

- **Image first.** Image leads, text follows to support it; weight at the top. In landscape, split side-by-side (image half read first). Never let an image interrupt the text chain.
- **One unbroken reading chain:** label → image → headline → subhead → body → details. Headline group stays tight to the image; practical details anchor the bottom edge with a modest pause, never a void.
- **Proportion:** golden-section guides (61.8% in from each edge) for major divisions; a single focal subject sits horizontally centered on the upper golden line — never dead center. With text, keep the image under about half the page height (diagonal crops may reach lower because they remove area).
- **Full bleed by default;** bleed symmetrically or not at all. Inset only for production limits.
- **Surplus space:** absorb it by scaling the image (to its cap) then the headline (more lines at larger size) — don't redistribute it into gaps. Type-only pieces anchor the text block low with one clean field above.
- **Strict grid, consistent margins sized from the shorter side.** Reflow by restructuring for the aspect ratio and re-setting line breaks per format; never scale one recipe from the width. Every format must be beautiful, not just fit.
- **Series:** vary layouts per image, keep the brand language constant, add one meaningful recurring signature (e.g., a large exhibition numeral or a real logo), aligned to the grid.
- **Direction words.** "Flush left," "image half first" and similar rules describe left-to-right scripts. For right-to-left or mixed content, translate them to *start* and *end* and see `scripts-and-direction.md`; Latin-only rules (tracked caps, no italics) do not transfer to scripts that have no such concept.

## Type defaults (L1)

- **Roles:** display face for the headline only; a text-optimized companion for the one promoted practical detail (e.g., dates); a neutral sans for everything else.
- **Scale:** dramatic jump from headline to the rest; moderate even steps below. Supporting text at one regular weight — no bold subheads. Emphasis by **weight within one family** (on the phrase that carries the meaning; modifiers lighter), moderate jumps, **never italics** for emphasis.
- **Type-only pieces:** the headline carries the image's job — push to extreme scale, stopping just short of full width.
- **Leading:** headline as tight as possible without any collision, but tight enough to read as one thought; body moderate. **Measure:** max ~55–75 characters per line. **Alignment:** flush left, ragged right; never justify.
- **Case:** tracked all-caps only for the smallest metadata tier, applied to the whole tier; promoted details stay sentence case. Small caps get moderate-to-generous tracking; display type sits close.
- Break headlines by phrase; balance lines; no widows/orphans. Judge a face by the actual glyphs in the copy. Character without quirkiness or robotic coldness; readability beats elegance.

## Color defaults (L1)

- Color marks hierarchy: the primary hue on the headline (whole element, one color), a scarce accent on the promoted detail, everything else neutral (metadata gray). Never a lone colored text element in print — in UI that signals a link.
- Pull exact hues from the imagery; never near-duplicates. A hierarchy color must clearly read as a color, not near-black.
- Temperature follows the concept: neutral/institutional → cool lead + warm accent; warm/inviting subjects → one warm family.
- Never pure black on pure white. Contrast is a floor, then a mood dial (secondary text may dim toward the floor).
- Dark versions use a deep colored field from the primary hue (not gray), white headline, the warm accent kept. Gradients only subtle and tonal by default.

## Motion defaults (L1 unless noted)

- Always eased; entrances **ease out** with a gentle landing (no slow start, no hard snap). Smooth but brisk.
- Build in reading order, one meaning unit at a time; the headline arrives as one unit. Direct motion — no anticipation, overshoot or follow-through by default.
- Hold every frame for full reading time; keep long holds alive with a slow eased push-in (anchored so image features move away from overlaid text). Lateral camera moves only when they reveal more of the story.
- Exits exist only to hand off: continue the direction of travel into the next frame; if nothing follows, don't exit (build once, breathe). Sequences hand off with motion — not cuts, not dissolves. Steady tempo.
- Let the concept inform the hero motion (literal or, preferably, metaphorical); contrast rules apply to the resolved state.
- With music: snap transitions to the beat. With voiceover: the voice drives the edit. No sound effects by default.
- Interface motion (state changes, menus, dialogs) is a different regime — short, eased-out, purposeful, with a reduced-motion variant. See `ui-craft.md`.

## Tonal presets (L2)

| Register | Display type | Color | Motion | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Quiet / premium | Warm editorial serif with a real weight range; light lead-in, medium core | Restrained, muted-to-mid saturation | Calm fade-and-rise, gentle build | Default for contemplative, cultural subjects |
| Playful | Friendly rounded sans | Brighter, more hues; solid pills/badges behind labels and dates | Spring/bounce allowed | Still square to the grid; headline one color |
| Energetic | Strong sans | Deep cool field, white type, bright warm accent | Faster, bigger travel, crisp wipe/mask reveals, no bounce | Discipline kept |
| Luxury | High-contrast Didone at full display scale | Deep jewel-toned field from the imagery, gold accent | Calm | Restraint in ornament, never in hierarchy |
| Warm / inviting | Editorial serif | One warm family from the imagery | Calm | Food, gathering, hospitality |
| Product / utility *(OD)* | Neutral sans, sentence-case headings | Neutral surfaces; one accent reserved for the primary action and links; closed set of status colors | State changes only, short, eased-out | Calm product UI, dashboards, settings, docs. Whitespace separates first, hairline second, card last |
| Broadsheet *(OD)* | Strong serif headlines with decisive scale jumps; serif for running text | Near-neutral ink and paper; one link color, applied at rest | Almost none | Dense editorial and news. Hairlines and whitespace instead of boxes |
| Paper / document *(OD)* | Serif sized for hierarchy | Warm off-white, one ink accent, shared warm neutrals | None or one calm fade-and-rise | Resumes, one-pagers, white papers, print-first decks |
| Showcase *(OD)* | Large, calm; steps back from the photograph | Interface nearly invisible; photograph carries color; accent on the primary action only | Slow push-in; mask or fade reveals | Product-photo-first, cinematic. Chrome near zero |
| Instrument *(OD)* | Neutral sans labels; tabular face for numbers | Deep tinted (not gray) dark field; every hue carries a fixed meaning | Signals and alerts only | Consoles, telemetry, trading. No glow or translucency |

Full detail for the five `OD` registers is in `references/brand-and-registers.md`. Sensibility (timeless, trend-forward, nostalgic) is a concept choice — execute any of them convincingly. Imperfection (hand-made, glitch) only when the concept asks; precise and digital otherwise.

## Imagery, material, icons, data, UI (L1)

- The medium follows the concept (a photography show uses the photographs). Image quality must match the subject's caliber; stylize (e.g., duotone) only to rescue a weak placeholder, never someone's showcased work. Present professional photography as shot (corrective retouching only). Prefer shallow depth of field — captured in camera, never faked. Crop to keep the concept's cause and effect in frame.
- Flat and simple; no glows, drop shadows, bevels, emboss, extrusion. Effects only for legibility or concept-in-motion. Interactive elevation (card lift + shadow on hover) is the UI exception. Texture: clean by default; fine grain over everything when warranted; never simulated materials.
- Type over busy imagery: gradient scrim first (a barely-there shadow may refine it), solid sampled-color panel as backup; shadow alone never. Captions sit on the image, small and dimmed (not below the contrast floor), in the least competing corner.
- Icons beside text: thin line icons matched to the type weight, colored with their text (filled icons for UI controls). No ornament or background patterns; a plain hairline rule occasionally.
- Data: conventional clear charts (axis, light grid, labels); decorate one storytelling point only; big number + supporting line for fast reads; avoid dense pictograms. A label beside a big number is vertically centered on the figure's optical height (cap/figure top to baseline), never baseline-aligned. Density follows the channel: glance media minimal, posters moderate, reference media dense.
- UI states transition (never instant swaps); purposeful motion such as a fill sweep or arrow nudge.

## Interface floor (imported defaults; apply to any UI)

Full rules and reasoning in `references/ui-craft.md`. Before showing an interface, check:

- **Five states** exist, not just the populated one: loading, empty, error, populated, edge (longest text, zero and thousands of items, missing data).
- **Keyboard focus** is visible on every interactive element and distinct from hover; state is never carried by hue alone; non-text controls meet a 3:1 contrast floor against their ground.
- **Targets** are comfortably large with separated hit areas; native elements first; reading order equals DOM order.
- **Forms**: a visible label (never placeholder-as-label), errors after the field is left and cleared the instant it's valid, one primary action per view.
- **Motion** has a job, is eased-out, and has a reduced-motion variant. No more than three flashes in any second, in UI or MP4.
- **Content is real**: no invented statistics, testimonials, logos or lorem ipsum; a named real thing gets its real image or an honestly labelled placeholder.

## Dealbreakers (never, unless the user explicitly asks)

Faux bold/italic · stretched type · straight quotes and hyphens for dashes · widows/orphans · justified text and rivers · letterspaced lowercase · too many typefaces · long centered paragraphs · all-caps body · cramped body leading · small text on busy images without support · glyph collisions · italic emphasis in display serifs · quirky novelty display faces · robotic serifs · hairline Didones outside luxury · faked outline strokes (outline styles only from a real font) · emoji where an icon belongs · floating 3D shapes · pill buttons everywhere · generic stock 3D illustration · over-rounded everything · decorative motifs and background patterns · bevel/emboss/drop-shadow effects · simulated paper texture · faked depth of field · amateur imagery for professional subjects · decorated charts (gradient bars, icon/value on every bar) · vibrating complements · muddy low-contrast palettes · pure black on pure white · blush pink + sage · near-duplicate hues · elastic drop-ins · spin-ins · zooms with lens flares/light leaks · attention shakes · word-by-word pops · dipping to black between every transition · instant color-only hover states · near-tangents.

**Explicit request only:** holiday red/green (tasteful), rainbow gradients, teal-and-orange (as a footage grade only), typewriter and scramble text effects, centered layouts, bento grids, icon-in-circle feature rows, gradient-blob heroes, glassmorphism, sparkle/hype copy, gradient headline text. **Sparingly:** tech purple-to-pink gradients.

A brand file may *mandate* a style-level trait from these lists (for example a capsule button or a gradient hero) for that brand's own work; use it only there, list it in the output as a brand-mandated exception, and never extend it elsewhere. Craft-level dealbreakers (faux bold/italic, stretched type, fake dashes, justified text, widows, collisions, faked depth of field) are never waived by a brand (`brand-and-registers.md`). If the user explicitly requests a listed style, execute it well (`brand-and-registers.md`, section D).

## Pre-flight checklist (run before showing any work)

- [ ] Register chosen from the concept; brand guidelines applied where they exist; conflicts with non-negotiables flagged.
- [ ] Reading chain is unbroken and image-first (or type-led with a clean field above).
- [ ] Every edge on the grid; any deviation is bold and deliberate; no near-tangents (including against image features).
- [ ] Image under about half the page height; no pooled voids; surplus absorbed by image/headline.
- [ ] Headline broken by phrase, balanced, no collisions; body ≤ ~75 characters per line; no widows.
- [ ] Large elements paired with smaller text are optically centered (e.g., big number + label).
- [ ] Color only on headline + promoted detail; hues sampled from the imagery; no near-duplicates; no pure black on white.
- [ ] Contrast measured against the real background for every text element (including over photos and gradients).
- [ ] Motion: eased-out entrances, reading-order build, full reading-time holds, exits that hand off, steady tempo.
- [ ] Nothing from the dealbreaker list.
- [ ] Every format/aspect ratio reflowed and re-set, not just scaled.
- [ ] Interfaces: the interface floor above passes; deliverable-specific checks from `formats.md` done.
- [ ] Non-Latin or multilingual content: direction, script type behavior and text expansion handled (`scripts-and-direction.md`).
- [ ] Nothing invented: every number, name, quote and image is real, supplied, or labelled placeholder.

When a situation isn't covered, reason from the core tenets, then check `references/index.md` for the nearest category, and cite the rounds in `references/evidence.md` if you need his exact words.

# Design Taste: Brand Flexibility

> Layer tags: `L1` foundation (always), `L2` tonal preset (only for that tone), `L3` brand-negotiable. `Rnnn` = the comparison round that produced the rule (see ../evidence.md). Non-negotiables in SKILL.md survive any brand override.

- **Respect the brand typeface over personal taste.** When guidelines mandate a typeface, use it. Don't swap in a preferred face, even for the headline. Apply the house principles inside the brand's type, such as hierarchy, weight emphasis, spacing and measure. `L3` · R087
- **When a brand rule breaks a non-negotiable, adjust minimally and flag it.** Example: a brand color that fails contrast on text. Keep the brand's intent, and change only what the non-negotiable requires, such as darkening the color only where text needs contrast. Tell the client about the conflict explicitly. Never ship the failing version silently, and never use the conflict as a pretext to override other brand rules. `L3` · R009, R087
- **The non-negotiables that survive any brand override:**
  1. Accessible text contrast.
  2. Every frame holds long enough to read all of its text.
  3. Text links are colored and underlined in UI.
  4. No glyph collisions and no near-tangents.
  5. Reading order and enforced hierarchy.

  *(Proposed in R087 and not contested.)*
- **Brand guidelines override personal color and image-treatment preferences.** If a brand document fixes the palette or prescribes a photographic look, it wins over taste-driven choices such as sampling colors from the image or grading naturally. Only the non-negotiables survive the override: accessible contrast and reading time. `L3` · R061, R066
- **Non-negotiable: in motion, hold every frame long enough to read all of its text.** R046
- **Non-negotiable: accessible text contrast.** If a brand palette would produce text that fails contrast standards, flag it and fix the pairing. Don't comply silently. `L1` · R009 (partial — other non-negotiables still to probe)

<!-- file: references/principles/color.md -->
# Design Taste: Color

> Layer tags: `L1` foundation (always), `L2` tonal preset (only for that tone), `L3` brand-negotiable. `Rnnn` = the comparison round that produced the rule (see ../evidence.md). Non-negotiables in SKILL.md survive any brand override.

- **Go fully neutral or commit to a considered palette. Never use a lone token accent.** Type set entirely in neutrals is clean and acceptable. A multi-hue system applied structurally across several elements, including the ground, makes a piece feel finished and is preferred when color is used. Several hues are welcome. What fails is the in-between: a single colored text element on an otherwise neutral page reads as odd. `L1` · R033
- **Color in type marks hierarchy, and it goes to the same two moments as the special typefaces.** The primary hue goes on the headline. A secondary accent goes on the promoted practical information, such as the date. The subhead, body and metadata stay in the neutral ink. This mirrors the type system, where the display serif and text serif mark those same two elements, so face and color reinforce one structure. `L1` · R034
- **A hierarchy color must clearly read as a color.** Type color that sits so dark and desaturated that it nearly matches the neutral ink fails at its job, because the distinction disappears. Push the hue just far enough from the ink to be unmistakable, while keeping it restrained. `L1` · R035
- **Restrained saturation for quiet subjects.** Between muted and mid: clearly colored, never loud. `L2 · quiet/premium` · R035 (bolder briefs not yet tested)
- **Palette temperature follows the concept.** For neutral or institutional subjects, lead cool for trust with a warm accent on the promoted detail (R036). When the concept and imagery are themselves warm and inviting, such as food, gathering or hospitality, stay within one warm family: a warm lead with a related warm accent (R061). In every case, choose hues deliberately for their psychological associations and pull them from the imagery. The color-role rules still hold: one color per element, accent scarce, metadata neutral. `L2` · R036, R061
- **Color is spent only where it means something.** Hue goes to the headline and the promoted detail, and nowhere else. Metadata and other minor tiers stay in neutral gray. Don't extend the primary hue into tints and shades for lesser elements, and don't wash the ground in a pale tint of it. Coloring the metadata calls attention to things that don't need it. `L1` · R037
- **Contrast is a floor, then a mood dial.** Accessible contrast is the hard minimum. Above it, contrast is an expressive tool: secondary text such as body and metadata can be dimmed toward the floor to set a quieter, moodier tone, on light or dark grounds alike. The headline and the promoted detail keep full strength. `L1` · R038
- **Going dark means a colored field, not gray.** When a piece moves to a dark ground, the primary hue becomes the field: a deep version of the brand's cool color, not a neutral near-black. Type then flips to white, with the headline in white. Dark and light versions are separate color designs, not inversions. Color roles get reassigned for the dark ground rather than carried over unchanged. Whether to go dark depends on the imagery, for example a dim photograph. `L1` · R038, R039
- **The accent stays scarce.** The warm accent works because it occupies a small area, the one promoted detail. Moving it onto the headline, a large mass, floods the piece with warmth and loses the contrast that made it work. Accent area stays small relative to the primary and neutral areas, on light or dark grounds. `L1` · R040
- **The warm accent survives the move to dark.** On a deep cool field, keep the warm accent on the promoted detail. Its temperature contrast breaks up the sameness of white-on-blue, which a white or cool-shifted accent fails to do. `L1` · R039
- **Pull exact hues from the imagery. Never use near-duplicates.** When type or graphics share a hue family with the image or illustration, use the image's actual color rather than a slightly different one. Two blues that are almost the same read as a mistake, the color equivalent of a near-tangent. Either match exactly or contrast clearly. `L1` · R057
- **One element, one color.** *(Holds in playful work too: R057.)* Never split a color within a single element, for example coloring only the emphasized part of a headline. Weight already handles emphasis inside the headline, so color applies to the headline as a whole unit. `L1` · R034
- **Tint the background only when the imagery calls for it.** A tinted ground is a mood decision, and it should be drawn from, and judged against, the actual photograph's palette. Plain paper is the default. Tint when the image suggests it. `L2/L3` · R034
- **In interactive work, a lone text accent means "actionable."** One color singled out on text reads as a link or call to action, because that's the convention. Reserve that treatment for actionable items in web or UI contexts, and don't use it decoratively in print or static pieces. `L1` · R033
- **Never pure black on pure white.** Full black on full white vibrates. Use a warm off-black ink on an off-white ground, as the house palette does, or deep colored fields. `L1` · R083
- **Accessible contrast is non-negotiable.** Text must meet proper contrast-ratio standards against whatever is behind it. Color and placement decisions are made inside that limit, never at its expense. `L1` · **non-negotiable** · R009

<!-- file: references/principles/composition-and-structure.md -->
# Design Taste: Composition & Structure

> Layer tags: `L1` foundation (always), `L2` tonal preset (only for that tone), `L3` brand-negotiable. `Rnnn` = the comparison round that produced the rule (see ../evidence.md). Non-negotiables in SKILL.md survive any brand override.

- **Structure must look intentional, and alignment is the proof of intent.** Every element should share an edge or axis with something else so the eye can sense the system holding it in place. Placement that relies on "feel" without a visible governing logic reads as accidental, even when it was considered. Default to a modular structure; any departure from it has to be legible as a decision, not drift. `L1` · R001
- **Build the reading order as a clear top-down sequence:** the image establishes context, then a dominant headline, then the subhead tucked directly beneath it as one unit, then supporting copy set alongside at a clearly subordinate scale. Each step should be obvious without the viewer having to search. `L1` · R001
- **One unbroken reading path, in strict rank order.** Arrange elements so the eye travels a single continuous chain: label → image → headline → subhead → body → details. Each element should hand off directly to the next. Nothing should sit outside the chain where it can be read early or out of sequence. A side-by-side placement is only acceptable if it doesn't open a second entry point. `L1` · R001, R002
- **Image first is a firm rule, not an accident of one layout.** The image leads, and the text follows to support and explain it. That puts the visual weight at the top, which feels grounded, as if the piece hangs from a strong anchor. Bottom-heavy arrangements feel strange. Confirmed in a direct test against two alternatives. `L1` · R002, R014
- **Consolidate all text into one unbroken block, footer details included.** The headline, subhead, body and practical details form one continuous group. Details stranded at the far edge of the page, separated from the body by a gap, don't get read. Keeping them in the block leads the eye straight into the critical practical information. `L1` · R018 (in image layouts, a modest pause before bottom-anchored details is fine; see R019)
- **Collect negative space into one deliberate field, outside the reading chain.** In a type-only piece, anchor the text block low and let one clean field sit above it. That field plays the role an image would, and the piece reads as top-down: field, then text. `L1` · R018
- **With an image, the image is the field: text hugs it, and details anchor the bottom edge.** The handoff from image to headline stays direct. Pushing extra space between them breaks the image's lead into the text. Practical details sit at the bottom edge, and a modest pause above them is fine, as long as it doesn't grow into a void that strands them. `L1` · R019
- **Absorb surplus by scaling content up, not by moving the space around.** When gaps grow too large, don't relocate the leftover space. Enlarge the primary elements until the gaps are proportionate: first the image, up to its height cap, then the headline, for example by breaking it into more lines at a larger size. The aim is for the footer pause to read as a deliberate rest that's no larger than the composition's other major gaps. `L1` · R005, R019
- **Never let an image interrupt the text chain.** Once reading starts, headline → subhead → body must stay contiguous. Splitting the text group around an image forces the reader to jump a gap mid-thought and makes the image feel like an intrusion. `L1` · R014
- ~~Supporting copy sits beside the primary block.~~ *Revised in R002:* body copy placed beside the headline creates a competing entry point and breaks the chain. Supporting copy follows the subhead sequentially. R001 → R002
- **Balance is a vehicle for the reading path, not a preference in itself.** Centered symmetry and an asymmetric split both work when they deliver a linear flow, and both fail when they don't. Choose the balance that best serves the sequence and the assets. When to choose centered vs. split is likely set by tone; see TONE. `L1` · R002
- **Give every element its own rank, and make each rank look like its role.** *(Refined by R024: distinguish the ranks through size and tone, not bold weight.)* Prefer a finely graduated hierarchy: label, headline, subhead, body and details each get a distinct treatment through size, weight or tone, and even the minor details are ranked among themselves. A subhead has to read unmistakably as a subhead, clearly below the headline and clearly above the body. Collapsing levels into one shared style flattens the piece. `L1` · R003
- **Ceiling on hierarchy depth.** Roughly one distinct level per content role is the upper limit. Going finer than that becomes fussy, because levels stop being distinguishable from each other. `L1` · R003 (soft ceiling — not yet tested beyond)
- **Whitespace must look placed, never left over.** Surplus space that pools in one spot, especially a dead band between the last content block and the footer, reads as a mistake. `L1` · R004, R005
- **Surplus space goes to the primary visual first, but only up to a point.** Grow the dominant element, such as the image, to absorb spare space. Don't spread the surplus evenly between groups, because that loosens the groups and makes the piece feel slack. Stop growing before the image starts crowding the text below. When it begins to dominate rather than lead, it reads as aggressive. In a text-bearing vertical layout, keep the image clearly under half the page height. Getting close to half feels uncomfortable, while sitting comfortably below it feels right. This held across two separate rounds. `L1` · R005, R009
- **The handoff from image to text needs more breathing room than the gaps within the text.** The first text element below an image should sit noticeably further from the image's edge than text elements sit from each other. Otherwise the text looks jammed against the picture. `L1` · R009
- **Use classical proportion systems as the scaffold for major divisions.** Size and place major zones with golden-ratio or rule-of-thirds relationships rather than arbitrary values, because these divisions are perceptually pleasing for well-understood reasons. Working method: set golden-section guides at 61.8% in from each of the four edges. The intersections they form mark where key visual elements should anchor. This is used most rigorously in print, but kept in mind for all work. `L1` · R004, R005
- **Never place a focal element at the dead geometric center.** The perceived center of a page sits above its true center, so an element placed at exact center looks like it's sagging. Lift it north of center. `L1` · R006
- **Mix strategies across axes: center on one, offset by proportion on the other.** For a single focal subject, horizontal centering is welcome. The vertical position comes from proportion. Symmetry and proportional placement are tools to combine, not rival systems. `L1` · R006, R007
- **The upper golden-section line is the default resting height for a focal subject.** It sits 38.2% down from the top. Just above center still feels low, and the upper third line feels too high, as if the subject is floating off the top. When the two systems disagree, the golden section wins over thirds. This was confirmed blind: his eye picked the golden line before the guides were shown. `L1` · R006, R007
- **Guides are a reference, not a snap target.** Putting a subject squarely on a thirds or golden-section intersection doesn't make the placement right by itself. The guides suggest where to start, and the eye makes the final call. `L1` · R006
- **Let imagery bleed. Full bleed is the default.** An image that runs off the page edges feels immersive. One held inside the margins feels like a picture placed on a page. Use an inset image only when production forces it, such as printing without bleed capability. That is a technical fallback, not an aesthetic choice. `L1` · R008
- **Commit to a bleed fully, or not at all.** A one-sided bleed, where an image breaks one edge while staying inset on the other, reads as a half-decision and is rejected. If an image bleeds, it bleeds symmetrically on the axis it breaks, and preferably reaches every edge it's near. `L1` · R008
- **Scale contrast is set by what else is carrying the piece.** When an image or graphic is the visual anchor, the headline leads at a confident but moderate scale. When type is the only visual, the headline must take on the image's job: push it to an extreme scale, while everything else stays small. Contrast grows as the other visual anchors are removed. `L1` · R005, R010
- **Stop the headline just short of the full width.** Even at extreme scale, the longest line shouldn't run margin to margin. Leave a visible margin of air so the headline feels confident rather than crammed into the frame. `L1` · R012
- **Deviate decisively or not at all.** Any departure from the orthogonal grid system, whether an angle, a bleed or an offset, must be large enough to read as unmistakably deliberate. A small deviation reads as an accident or an error. A bold one reads as a choice. When in doubt, stay on the system. This is the cross-cutting rule behind several rounds: the one-sided bleed was rejected, loose placement was rejected, and the subtle diagonal "seems like an accident." `L1` · R001, R008, R013
- **Orthogonal is the safe default. A diagonal is a context-dependent accent.** A level, orthogonal structure is always acceptable. A strong diagonal cut can add energy when the image and brand support it. Whether to use one is a brand and imagery decision, not a universal rule. `L2/L3` · R013
- **A diagonal must relate to something else in the composition.** An angle earns its place when it echoes or responds to another element, such as the shape the headline's line breaks make. An angle that relates to nothing looks arbitrary. `L1` · R013
- **Dead wedges left by geometry count as wasted whitespace.** When a diagonal crop leaves an open wedge, extend the shape so its lowest point comes down toward the content below. The image's visual mass, not just its bounding edge, is what the "under half the page" rule protects. A diagonal can reach lower because it removes area. `L1` · R013 (partial)
- **Clean separation by default. Flat overlap is the alternate.** Text sitting cleanly below the image is the default. A flat text panel that rises into the image, with its edges on the page margins and the image continuing behind it, is a legitimate alternate. It ties the image and text together more tightly, and the choice between them is a brand and imagery call. Layering is done with flat overlap, never simulated depth. `L1` default · `L2/L3` alternate · R015
- **Crop for the concept: keep the cause and the effect in frame.** Framing is decided by what the piece is about. If the story is a relationship, like a light source and what it falls on, the crop must include both ends of it, which usually means a wider, environmental frame. A tight crop that keeps the effect but loses its source cuts the idea in half. Other subjects get different crops. `L1` · R020
- **No near-tangents.** Two elements that almost touch, especially corner to corner, create an awkward, nervous tension. Either give them clear separation or make them deliberately align or overlap. This applies to text over imagery too: check overlaid labels against the features in the picture, such as window corners and edges, not just against the page grid. `L1` · R020
- **Repetition still needs a lead.** When several like elements repeat, such as images in a set, rank them. One featured element establishes the scene, and smaller ones support it with closer details, like an establishing shot followed by inserts. Equal repetition is monotonous. `L1` · R021
- **Frame images in proportions real imagery can fill.** Avoid extreme slivers or unusual aspect ratios for image zones. They force awkward crops and make sourcing or generating the asset hard. A layout is only good if it can actually be produced with real content. `L1` · R002



---

<!-- file: references/principles/consistency-across-a-series.md -->
# Design Taste: Consistency Across a Series

> Layer tags: `L1` foundation (always), `L2` tonal preset (only for that tone), `L3` brand-negotiable. `Rnnn` = the comparison round that produced the rule (see ../evidence.md). Non-negotiables in SKILL.md survive any brand override.

- **Vary the layout. Keep the brand language constant.** A series should show real variety from piece to piece, with different layouts suited to each image, while clearly reading as one brand. The type system, color logic, hierarchy, label system and voice hold steady. Variety in structure, consistency in language. `L1` · R078
- **Variation must be decisive.** If pieces are nearly identical in layout, small per-piece swaps, such as different headline colors, read as inconsistency rather than intent. Either hold a template strictly or vary meaningfully. This is the series form of "deviate decisively." `L1` · R013, R078
- **A recurring signature element strengthens a series.** One element that repeats across every piece, like a large exhibition numeral, adds design and branding without fighting the variety. It must be meaningful (a real number, or a real logo). A typeset name standing in for a logo is weak; use the actual logo if one exists. Align the signature to the grid, for example flush with the text's left edge, or set it over the photograph. It should never float in a leftover spot. `L1` · R079
- **Never shrink the image to a token.** Even in a type-led variant, a small inset thumbnail photo is a weak treatment. The image keeps a substantial, intentional presence. `L1` · R078



---

<!-- file: references/principles/contrast-and-hierarchy.md -->
# Design Taste: Contrast & Hierarchy

> Layer tags: `L1` foundation (always), `L2` tonal preset (only for that tone), `L3` brand-negotiable. `Rnnn` = the comparison round that produced the rule (see ../evidence.md). Non-negotiables in SKILL.md survive any brand override.

- **A strong second voice is welcome. A tie is not.** A headline can be pushed up to nearly rival the image, which adds interest, but the image should still edge it out. When the headline grows, give the image a little more height to keep it in the lead. Two focal points work as a clear first and a close second, not as equals. `L1` · R016, R017
- **Emphasis follows the piece's job.** Functional information the audience needs to act on, like dates on a flyer, deserves more emphasis than its default rank as a detail. Promote it in proportion: enough to be found quickly, never enough to compete with the headline. `L1` · R016, R017
- **Promote by size, not by relocation.** Raise important information by giving it a moderate size step within its natural place in the reading order, for example the date on its own line in the footer. A smaller bump that keeps it aligned in the detail row is also acceptable. Don't move it somewhere more prominent but out of sequence. `L1` · R017
- **Hierarchy is enforced, not discovered.** The viewer should never wonder what to read first. Rank between levels should be unmistakable, and the spatial order should match the rank order. This held in every tonal register tested (quiet, playful, energetic, luxury, warm): tone changes the voice, never the enforcement. `L1` · R001, R002, R056–R061



---

<!-- file: references/principles/core-tenets.md -->
# Design Taste: Core Tenets

> Layer tags: `L1` foundation (always), `L2` tonal preset (only for that tone), `L3` brand-negotiable. `Rnnn` = the comparison round that produced the rule (see ../evidence.md). Non-negotiables in SKILL.md survive any brand override.

These recur across many rounds and override stylistic defaults:
0. **Concept drives execution. Always. But the design principles still hold.** The subject and its imagery choose the voice: typeface, palette temperature, motion energy, crop, camera. The foundation rules never bend: hierarchy, reading order, contrast, reading time, intentionality and restraint in structure. Every L2 preset below is a consequence of this tenet, not a style to apply by default. (R011, R020, R051, R056–R061)
1. **Everything must read as intentional.** Every placement, deviation, color and motion choice must be visibly deliberate. Anything that could be mistaken for an accident or a default is wrong, even if it's technically fine. (R001, R008, R013, R022, R050)
2. **Hierarchy is enforced, and it follows meaning.** The reader never wonders what comes first. Rank, weight, color and motion order all follow the content's meaning and reading order. (R001–R003, R014, R027, R034, R043)
3. **Restraint over effect.** Moderate steps, no gratuitous bold, no bounce, no shadows, no lone accents. Drama is concentrated in one place, the headline or image, and everything else stays calm. (R024, R027, R031, R041, R048, R015)
4. **Legibility is non-negotiable.** Accessible contrast, enough reading time in motion, no glyph collisions, no near-tangents. (R009, R020, R029, R046)
5. **Decide by the concept and the real assets.** Crops, camera moves, tints and dark modes are chosen for what this subject and this photograph need. (R020, R034, R038, R047)



---

<!-- file: references/principles/cultural-reference-sensibility.md -->
# Design Taste: Cultural / Reference Sensibility

> Layer tags: `L1` foundation (always), `L2` tonal preset (only for that tone), `L3` brand-negotiable. `Rnnn` = the comparison round that produced the rule (see ../evidence.md). Non-negotiables in SKILL.md survive any brand override.

- **Avoid effects that date a piece.** Treatments strongly tied to a past era of digital design, like bevel-and-emboss and heavy drop shadows, are avoided. `L1` · R064
- **Sensibility is a concept choice. Be fluent in all of them.** Timeless and original, trend-forward, and nostalgic or reference-heavy are all valid registers, chosen by the concept. Trend-forward editorial work (oversized tight grotesks, mono labels, exposed grids, acid accents) is admired as cool and modern. The agent must be able to execute each sensibility convincingly, with the foundation rules intact. Being dated by accident is the failure; choosing a period deliberately is fine. `L2` · R064, R080



---

<!-- file: references/principles/data-information-design.md -->
# Design Taste: Data / Information Design

> Layer tags: `L1` foundation (always), `L2` tonal preset (only for that tone), `L3` brand-negotiable. `Rnnn` = the comparison round that produced the rule (see ../evidence.md). Non-negotiables in SKILL.md survive any brand override.

- **Conventional, clear charts by default.** A proper axis, light gridlines, axis labels and every category labeled. This reads as the cleanest. Ultra-minimal data-ink that strips the axis is less preferred, and so is decorating every mark. Keep values off individual bars unless they're being called out. `L1` · R074
- **Form follows the message and the attention budget.**
  - **A trend:** show a progression over time with a conventional chart.
  - **The headline is one metric:** lead with one big number and a short supporting line. It's the fastest read with the least cognitive load, and the default for quick-hit contexts like social posts.
  - **Time allows:** sequence the two in motion, showing the chart and then transitioning to the big number to land the point.
  - **Pictograms:** use them sparingly. Many small repeated icons overwhelm and read as visual noise, like "a bunch of tiny bugs."

  `L1` · R075
- **Optically center a label beside a big number.** When a large figure sits beside a multi-line label, center the label block vertically on the figure's optical height, from cap or figure top to baseline. Don't baseline-align them, and don't center on the line box: either way the label sinks below the number. The same applies to any large element paired with smaller text. `L1` · V01
- **Decorate only to tell the story, and only once.** If one data point matters to the narrative, such as a record year, treat that single mark differently: a highlight color, an icon or a direct label. Decorating every mark makes nothing important, the same hierarchy logic as everywhere else. `L1` · R074



---

<!-- file: references/principles/density-and-information-load.md -->
# Design Taste: Density & Information Load

> Layer tags: `L1` foundation (always), `L2` tonal preset (only for that tone), `L3` brand-negotiable. `Rnnn` = the comparison round that produced the rule (see ../evidence.md). Non-negotiables in SKILL.md survive any brand override.

- **Density is set by the channel and the time available.**
  - **Glance media** (banner ads, social posts) get one message and minimal information. There are a second or two to win attention, so be direct and light.
  - **Posters and general pieces** sit in the moderate middle.
  - **Reference media** (itineraries, emails, programs) can carry dense, multi-message content, organized by the same hierarchy.

  There's a place for each. Pick by the channel and application. `L1` · R075, R077
- **Busy is often just one element too many.** Richness tips into busyness when the count of competing items passes what the hierarchy can organize. In a lead-plus-support grid, a lead and two supporting items reads as rich. Adding a fourth item of similar weight reads as busy. When a set feels crowded, cut an item before shrinking everything. `L1` · R021 (partial)



---

<!-- file: references/principles/grid-and-systemization.md -->
# Design Taste: Grid & Systemization

> Layer tags: `L1` foundation (always), `L2` tonal preset (only for that tone), `L3` brand-negotiable. `Rnnn` = the comparison round that produced the rule (see ../evidence.md). Non-negotiables in SKILL.md survive any brand override.

- **Reflow by relationships, not fixed sizes.** When a layout moves to another format, adjust type size and column widths to keep the comfortable measure and the hierarchy intact. Never scale one recipe from the width. `L1` · R003, R070
- **Restructure for the aspect ratio.** Portrait formats stack image over text. Landscape formats split side by side, with the image taking one half, which reads first, and the text the other. The reading order survives: image first, then the text chain. Size type and margins from the shorter side, so margins stay proportionally consistent across formats. `L1` · R070
- **Every format must be beautiful and legible, so re-set the copy per format.** When a format gets cramped, restore the breathing room by changing how the copy is set, not by squeezing the gaps. Re-break the headline into fewer lines, or set the subhead on one line. Line breaks are per-format decisions. Use judgment: an output that technically fits but feels cramped has failed. `L1` · R070
- **Strict grid by default, with deliberate deviation only.** Modular alignment and consistent margins are the default. Departures must be bold and intentional (see Composition). `L1` · R001, R013, R057, R069
- **Lean toward strict grid adherence.** Equal margins and shared column edges are what make a composition feel resolved. Intuitive or by-eye placement is a liability, not a style. `L1` · R001 (partial — still to test how much rule-breaking a strong grid can absorb)



---

<!-- file: references/principles/iconography-and-supporting-graphics.md -->
# Design Taste: Iconography & Supporting Graphics

> Layer tags: `L1` foundation (always), `L2` tonal preset (only for that tone), `L3` brand-negotiable. `Rnnn` = the comparison round that produced the rule (see ../evidence.md). Non-negotiables in SKILL.md survive any brand override.

- **Icons are welcome on practical information.** Small icons beside the date, location and entry details help scanning and add polish. `L1` · R068
- **Ornament and pattern must serve a purpose. By default, use none.** Decorative marks, motifs and background patterns add clutter even when they're drawn from the concept. A window-pane motif echoing the photo still reads as busy. Background patterns are distracting. The one acceptable structural ornament is a plain hairline rule, used occasionally to separate content groups, with no mark or flourish on it. `L1` · R069
- **Beside type, use thin line icons whose stroke matches the type weight.** Icons set alongside typography are drawn as thin lines, with stroke weight matched to the text they accompany and color taken from it, sized to the line. This holds about 70% of the time. Solid filled icons are reserved for UI contexts such as buttons and controls, where they need more presence. `L1` · R068



---

<!-- file: references/principles/imagery-and-photography.md -->
# Design Taste: Imagery & Photography

> Layer tags: `L1` foundation (always), `L2` tonal preset (only for that tone), `L3` brand-negotiable. `Rnnn` = the comparison round that produced the rule (see ../evidence.md). Non-negotiables in SKILL.md survive any brand override.

- **The medium follows the concept.** If the subject is photography, use the photography itself, meaning the actual work being promoted. Illustration is right when the piece communicates an experience or an idea rather than showcasing photographs. Stylized treatments sit between the two. `L1` · R065
- **Image quality must match the subject's caliber.** An amateur-looking photograph, with snapshot framing, phone-camera rendering or flat light, undermines a piece about professional work, however good the layout. Source imagery is judged as rigorously as the type. `L1` · R065
- **Prefer shallow depth of field, captured in camera, never faked.** Shallow focus draws the eye into the photograph, the way human vision blurs the periphery around what it's looking at. Favor it when choosing or directing imagery. It must come from the source photograph. Simulating blur in post is not acceptable, in line with the no-simulated-effects rule. `L1` · R067
- **Frame the subject by the composition rules (inferred).** Within a photograph, keep the concept's cause and effect in frame (R020), and favor golden-section placement of the focal subject over dead center (R006–R007). The image's share of the page stays under half (R005). `L1` · R005, R006, R007, R020 (inferred, not separately tested)
- **Respect the photographer's work: correct it, don't restyle it.** When the image is the subject, someone's professional photography, present it as shot. Apply only corrective retouching: proper exposure, and saturation that is neither pushed nor drained. No dramatic grades, crushed contrast or desaturation, unless brand guidelines prescribe a look. `L1` · R066
- **Type color comes from the photograph.** Sample the accent directly from tones in the image. Choose the primary hue to complement the photograph, rather than imposing a fixed house color that fights it. Fixed brand colors are the exception. `L1` · `L3` brand overrides · R057, R066
- **Stylization can rescue weak imagery.** When the available image is below the bar, a treatment such as a duotone in the palette's colors improves how it sits in the piece and unifies it with the system. Use it as a deliberate fix, not as a default look. `L1` · R065



---

<!-- file: references/principles/imperfection-and-authenticity.md -->
# Design Taste: Imperfection & Authenticity

> Layer tags: `L1` foundation (always), `L2` tonal preset (only for that tone), `L3` brand-negotiable. `Rnnn` = the comparison round that produced the rule (see ../evidence.md). Non-negotiables in SKILL.md survive any brand override.

- **Precise and digital by default. Imperfection only when the concept asks for it.** Hand-made marks and glitch or error aesthetics are legitimate tools for the right creative piece, but they must be read from the room. For refined, institutional or quiet subjects they don't belong. `L1` default · `L2` (concept-driven) · R081



---

<!-- file: references/principles/interaction-and-affordance.md -->
# Design Taste: Interaction & Affordance

> Layer tags: `L1` foundation (always), `L2` tonal preset (only for that tone), `L3` brand-negotiable. `Rnnn` = the comparison round that produced the rule (see ../evidence.md). Non-negotiables in SKILL.md survive any brand override.

- **Colored text signals interactivity.** In UI and web work, a single accent color on text is reserved for links and actionable items, and isn't spent on emphasis or decoration. `L1` · R033, R076
- **Text links: color and underline, always, at rest.** Follow UX best practice. A text link carries both signals, a distinct color and an underline, in its resting state. An underline that appears only on hover is not acceptable. `L1` · **non-negotiable in UI** · R076
- **State changes transition, never just swap.** Hover and press states should animate between states with the house brisk ease-out. An instant color-only change on a button is too plain. Purposeful motion, like a fill sweeping in or an arrow nudging toward the destination, is welcome. `L1` · R076
- **Elevation is a legitimate interactive affordance.** On the web, lifting a card toward the viewer on hover, with a slight rise, scale and shadow, literally pulls it out of the page and is a strong signal for cards and clickable surfaces. This is the UI exception to the no-shadow default, because there the shadow communicates state rather than decorating. Match the treatment to what is being activated. `L1` · R015, R064, R076



---

<!-- file: references/principles/material-texture-surface.md -->
# Design Taste: Material / Texture / Surface

> Layer tags: `L1` foundation (always), `L2` tonal preset (only for that tone), `L3` brand-negotiable. `Rnnn` = the comparison round that produced the rule (see ../evidence.md). Non-negotiables in SKILL.md survive any brand override.

- **Clean by default. When texture is used, use fine grain or noise over the whole piece.** Clean, flat surfaces are the default. When a piece calls for texture, the preferred treatment is a fine, unified grain or noise across everything, image and type together, as one coherent medium. Texture is a per-piece, concept-driven decision. `L1` default · R062
- **Gradients: welcome when careful, never overdone.** A subtle tonal gradient within a single hue, such as a field deepening away from the image, adds elegance and is the default gradient move. Two-hue gradients are acceptable, and can look very good, when the concept or the actual colors in the imagery suggest both hues. A gradient should be felt more than noticed. `L1` (subtle tonal) · `L2/L3` (multi-hue, imagery-driven) · R063
- **No simulated materials.** Faked paper tooth, fiber or other skeuomorphic substrate effects applied as a background are rejected. Texture should read as a property of the medium, like grain or noise, not an imitation of a physical material. `L1` · R062
- **Flat and simple is the elegant default.** Type and surfaces stay flat. Glows, drop shadows, bevels, emboss and extrusion read as gimmicky, and bevel-and-emboss with drop shadow reads as dated. `L1` · R015, R064
- **Effects are allowed for one of two reasons (plus interactive elevation, see Interaction).**
  - **Function:** a shadow or glow that is necessary for legibility, such as separating type from a busy image, or a panel over a full-page image.
  - **Concept in motion:** an effect that embodies the idea dynamically, such as a glow that blooms as part of an animation, or a shadow that shifts direction as a light source moves across the headline. Static decorative effects fail this test.

  Any effect must align with the concept and be executed with restraint and elegance. `L1` · R015, R051, R064
- **Texture and effects must carry meaning.** Surface treatments, whether grain, glow or dimension, are justified by the concept or the medium, never added as decoration. `L1` · R062, R064



---

<!-- file: references/principles/motion.md -->
# Design Taste: Motion

> Layer tags: `L1` foundation (always), `L2` tonal preset (only for that tone), `L3` brand-negotiable. `Rnnn` = the comparison round that produced the rule (see ../evidence.md). Non-negotiables in SKILL.md survive any brand override.

- **Always eased, never mechanical.** Every movement accelerates and decelerates. Linear or constant-speed motion is never used for design elements. `L1` · R041
- **Entrances ease out, with a gentle landing rather than a snap.** Elements arrive with momentum and decelerate smoothly into place. A slow start, as in ease-in or ease-in-out, reads as laggy. An exponential snap-stop reads as abrupt. The ideal is a moderate ease-out curve: responsive at the start and soft at the end. `L1` · R041, R042
- **Build in reading order, one meaning unit at a time.** Choreography is a sequential build that follows the reading chain: image, then label, headline, subhead, body, details. Each unit arrives in turn. But a unit that reads as one thought, such as a multi-line headline, enters as one piece, not line by line. Motion should respect the same semantic grouping the layout does. Everything arriving at once throws away the build. `L1` · R043
- **Elements enter with a fade and a gentle rise.** A short upward drift paired with a fade-in reads as elegant and suits quiet, refined pieces. Mask or wipe reveals and motionless fades are less fitting for this register. `L2 · quiet/premium` · R044 (other tones may call for different entries)
- **An exit is chosen by what comes next.** Exits serve continuity, not symmetry for its own sake.
  - If another frame follows with the same directional language, continue the motion: elements leave in the order they arrived, still traveling in the entry direction, so the next frame's build picks up the same vector.
  - If the piece is a single standalone frame, mirror the entry: reverse order, reverse direction.
  - Everything vanishing at once is the weakest choice in either case.

  Exits accelerate away, the counterpart of ease-out entrances. `L1` · R045
- **Always hold long enough to read everything.** A frame must stay fully resolved on screen long enough for an average reader to read every word in it, body copy included, before anything exits. This is **non-negotiable**, a legibility requirement in the same class as accessible contrast. Brisk motion applies to how things move, never to how long they stay. *Implication (provisional):* if the required hold makes a frame drag, reduce the copy on that frame or split it across frames. Don't shorten the hold. `L1` · **non-negotiable** · R046
- **Keep long holds alive with a slow push-in.** While type rests for its full reading time, the image can carry a slow, continuous push-in (the Ken Burns move), eased at both ends. It adds life without competing with reading. Anchor the push so image features move away from overlaid text rather than toward it. `L1` · R047
- **The camera only travels to reveal something.** A lateral pan or drift is justified only when it uncovers more of the story, for example more of the room the light falls on. A drift for its own sake is decoration. This is the motion counterpart of cropping for the concept. `L1` · R020, R047
- **Direct motion, with no cartoon principles, by default.** Elements travel straight to their resting place and stop. No anticipation dips, no overshoot, no follow-through settle. Classic animation exaggeration reads as less elegant in quiet and energetic work. Bounce and spring are fine when the concept is genuinely playful. `L1` default · `L2 · playful` exception · R041, R048, R058
- **Motion flexes with the concept.** The motion dials move with tone the same way the type and color dials do:
  - **Calm/quiet:** eased fade-and-rise and a gentle build.
  - **Energetic:** faster timing, bigger travel, crisp wipe and mask reveals and tighter stagger. Still eased, still no bounce.
  - **Playful:** spring and bounce allowed.

  The structural motion rules hold in every register: reading-order build, the headline as one unit, reading-time holds, exits that hand off, and steady tempo. `L2` · R044, R058
- **Nothing exits unless something follows.** A single piece of content, looping or not, builds in once and then stays, kept alive by slow ambient camera motion that breathes in and out. Exits exist only to hand off to what comes next. Building out and back in with nothing new to show is wasted motion. (This refines R045: the mirrored exit applies only when a standalone piece must end, such as at a cut in a longer edit.) `L1` · R045, R049
- **In sequences, frames hand off with motion.** Outgoing content exits in the direction of travel and incoming content builds in on the same vector, so the sequence reads as one continuous, considered movement. Hard cuts and slow crossfades read as default and unconsidered by comparison. Motion's primary job is to connect, carrying the eye from one idea to the next. Ambient motion such as the push-in keeps holds alive. `L1` · R045, R050
- **Pacing equals reading time plus brisk motion.** Transitions are quick and smooth, holds are as long as the copy requires, and nothing lingers in transition. `L1` · R041, R046, R050
- **Let the concept inform the hero motion.** Where the subject offers a motion idea, the hero element's entrance can interpret it, literally (light sweeping in to reveal) or metaphorically (type brightening like dawn). These creative interpretations are preferred to generic motion, with a slight lean toward the subtler, metaphorical reading. The house fade-and-rise is the fallback when the concept offers nothing, and supporting elements keep the house language either way. `L1` · R051
- **Contrast rules apply to resolved states.** A brief, deliberate low-contrast moment during an entrance, such as type brightening from faint, is acceptable. Every element must reach full accessible contrast before its reading hold begins. `L1` · R046, R051
- **Black is for structure, not transitions.** Fade in from black at the start and out to black at the end, or dip to black at a genuine break in the story. Dipping through black between every frame is a cheat. Frames hand off with motion instead (R050). `L1` · R050, R082
- **Keep tempo steady.** Every transition in a sequence moves at the same pace. Accelerations and deliberate tempo shifts are unnecessary complication, unless the motion is synchronized to music, in which case the music sets the tempo. `L1` · R052
- **Smooth, but brisk.** The character is soft, eased motion without the slow drift: gentle curves with a confident, moderate pace. Snappy, hard-stopping motion feels abrupt, and long, floating motion takes too long. No physics bounce or spring overshoot by default. `L1` · R041 (default character; tone presets may shift pace)

<!-- file: references/principles/negative-constraints.md -->
# Design Taste: Negative Constraints

> Layer tags: `L1` foundation (always), `L2` tonal preset (only for that tone), `L3` brand-negotiable. `Rnnn` = the comparison round that produced the rule (see ../evidence.md). Non-negotiables in SKILL.md survive any brand override.

- **Heavy condensed display type on a quiet or contemplative subject.** It reads as comical. Called "horrible". R011
- **Robotic, mechanical serifs.** Overly engineered or uniform serifs that lack warmth. R026
- **Fully justified text.** "I see no reason to fully justify text in any of my designs." R030
- **Shadow-only legibility fixes.** Drop shadows on type over a busy photo, used instead of a scrim or panel. Extremely difficult to read. R064, R071
- **Glyph collisions between lines.** Descenders hitting ascenders or i-dots in the next line, such as a *Q* tail striking the dot of an *i* or the top of a *t*. R025, R029
- **Dated effects: bevel and emboss, drop-shadowed extruded type.** Feels very dated. Also, static glows and shadows used as decoration. R064
- **Dense pictograms.** Rows of many tiny repeated icons. Overwhelming; reads like bugs on the page. R075
- **Decorated charts.** Gradient-filled bars (especially warm-to-cool gradients on data marks), an icon on every bar, a value on every bar. Overkill noise. R074
- **Decorative motifs and background patterns.** Marks centered on rules, corner ornaments, and repeating patterns behind text. Distracting, noisy clutter. R069
- **Faked photographic effects.** Simulated depth of field or blur added in post. R067
- **Amateur imagery for professional subjects.** Snapshot-quality photos with cheap phone-camera rendering in a piece about professional creative work. R065
- **Motion clichés, never used:** elastic drop-in bounces, spin-ins, slow dramatic zooms with lens-flare or light-leak overlays, attention shakes and wiggles, word-by-word scale pops, and dipping to black between every transition. These differ from what is accepted: a subtle spring is fine for genuinely playful concepts (R058), and a slow push-in on a hold is preferred (R047). The clichéd versions are the gratuitous, effect-for-effect's-sake forms. R082
- **Motion clichés, only when the concept truly calls for them:** typewriter reveals and scramble or decode effects. Never in quiet or refined work. R082
- **Color combinations to avoid:**
  - **Vibrating complements:** equally saturated opposing hues side by side.
  - **Muddy, murky, low-contrast palettes:** these are an accessibility failure.
  - **Pure black on pure white:** too vibrating.
  - **Blush pink and sage:** avoid entirely.

  R083
- **Color combinations only on explicit request:**
  - **Holiday red and green:** only when a holiday piece is explicitly asked for, and even then used tastefully.
  - **Rainbow gradients:** only when explicitly asked for.
  - **Teal and orange:** only as a requested color grade on footage or photography. Never as background and type colors.

  R083
- **Use sparingly:** tech purple-to-pink gradients. R083
- **Typographic crimes, never:** faux bold or italic (software-synthesized styles), stretched or squished letterforms, straight quotes and hyphens standing in for real quotes and dashes, widows and orphans, rivers in justified text, wide letterspacing on lowercase, too many typefaces in one piece, long centered paragraphs, all-caps body copy, cramped body leading, and small text on a busy image with no support. "Avoid all of these. These are really bad." R084
- **Outlined text only from the font itself.** Hollow or stroked type is occasionally acceptable when it comes from a typeface designed with an outline style. A stroke faked by the software is never acceptable, in line with the no-simulated-effects rule. R084
- **Generic, machine-made tells, never:**
  - Floating glossy 3D shapes.
  - Emoji where a proper icon belongs. Never use emoji as bullets or markers; use real icons drawn to the house icon rules.
  - Pill-shaped buttons and tags used everywhere.
  - Generic stock 3D character illustrations.
  - Over-rounded corners on everything.

  R085
- **Acceptable only on explicit request:** fully centered layouts, bento grids, icon-in-circle feature rows, gradient-blob heroes, glassmorphism, sparkle icons with hype copy, and gradient-filled headline text. Never reach for them by default. R085
- **Simulated paper texture.** Fake paper tooth or fiber as a background effect. R062
- **Italic emphasis in display serifs.** Collisions between ascenders and descenders, and a general preference for weight-based emphasis. R025
- **Display faces with quirky, idiosyncratic letterforms.** Odd glyph shapes that hurt readability, especially in letters like *h* and *f*. R011
- **Hairline Didone display serifs, outside luxury.** Extreme thick-thin contrast that makes text "extremely difficult to read" in quiet or editorial work (R012). The exception is luxury, where a Didone at large display size on a dark field is preferred (R060). Never use one at small sizes. R012, R060
- **Near-tangents.** Elements that almost touch, especially corner to corner, such as a label's last character nearly kissing a window corner in the image. R020

<!-- file: references/principles/sound-motion-sync.md -->
# Design Taste: Sound / Motion Sync

> Layer tags: `L1` foundation (always), `L2` tonal preset (only for that tone), `L3` brand-negotiable. `Rnnn` = the comparison round that produced the rule (see ../evidence.md). Non-negotiables in SKILL.md survive any brand override.

- **With music, transitions snap to the beat.** When a piece has a music bed, each transition waits for the next beat. That's enough to feel locked to the music without the long waits of phrase-level syncing. Snapping only ever extends holds, never shortens them, so the reading-time rule still governs. Without music, timing follows reading time alone, at a steady tempo. `L1` · R052, R053
- **With a voiceover, the voice drives the edit.** Each frame arrives as its line begins, so what is seen and heard land together. Letting the visuals lead by a beat is an acceptable alternative. Visuals running on their own schedule, unsynced to the voice, is not. The reading-time floor still applies: a frame never leaves before its text can be read, even if the line ends sooner. `L1` · R055
- **No sound effects by default.** The music bed carries the audio. Whooshes on transitions and ticks on entrances add nothing to a piece like this. Reserve sound effects for a brief whose tone genuinely calls for them. `L1` default · R054 (energetic or playful presets untested)

<!-- file: references/principles/text-image-relationship.md -->
# Design Taste: Text / Image Relationship

> Layer tags: `L1` foundation (always), `L2` tonal preset (only for that tone), `L3` brand-negotiable. `Rnnn` = the comparison round that produced the rule (see ../evidence.md). Non-negotiables in SKILL.md survive any brand override.

- **Small labels sit on the image by default rather than claiming their own band.** When an image bleeds to the top, overlay a minor label such as the kicker in a reversed color instead of pushing the image down or giving the label its own strip. Spending a whole band of the page on a tiny label wastes immersion. `L1` · R008, R009
- **Overlay only where contrast can be guaranteed. Otherwise move the text into the text zone.** If a label is essential to understanding the piece and the image can't guarantee accessible contrast behind it, relocate it to the solid text area. Legibility outranks immersion. `L1` · R009
- **Text on an image is limited to two cases: minor labels and large, clearly contrasting headlines.** Essential practical information, such as dates, places and calls to action, never sits on the image. It goes in the solid text zone where its legibility is guaranteed. A minor label can overlay because nothing breaks if it's missed. `L1` · R009, R017
- **Type over a busy photograph: gradient scrim first, solid panel as the backup.** When type must sit on imagery, darken the image behind it with a gradient that fades into the photo. The type stays clean and the image keeps its full bleed. If a scrim can't secure contrast, use a solid panel in a color sampled from the photo. A shadow on the type alone is never enough; it makes busy-background text extremely hard to read. A barely perceptible shadow combined with a gradient scrim is acceptable as a finishing touch, to nudge legibility while keeping the type looking clean. The scrim does the work, and the shadow only refines it. `L1` · R071
- **Captions sit on the image, quietly.** A caption identifying an image belongs on the image itself, as close as possible to what it describes. It's set small and slightly dimmed so it never distracts from the picture. Place it in the least competing corner, usually the lower right, where the eye finishes reading the image. The exact placement varies with each image. Dimming stops at the accessible contrast floor, as with the other secondary text (R038). `L1` · R072
- **In long-form layouts, set images beside the text, not in separate stacked blocks.** Placing an inset image alongside the copy, with the text wrapping around it, gives the body a comfortable measure and makes the page feel considered. An image stacked above full-width text is oversimplified, and the lines run long. A rectangular wrap is always acceptable. A shaped wrap, where the text follows a contour, is preferred when the shape comes from the concept, such as an arched window for a show about light and windows. `L1` (wrap) · `L2` (shaped, concept-driven) · R073
- **Overlay and image size are separate decisions.** Freeing space by overlaying a label doesn't mean the image should grow into it. Set the image size by proportion first, then decide where labels go. `L1` · R009

<!-- file: references/principles/tone-and-emotional-register.md -->
# Design Taste: Tone & Emotional Register

> Layer tags: `L1` foundation (always), `L2` tonal preset (only for that tone), `L3` brand-negotiable. `Rnnn` = the comparison round that produced the rule (see ../evidence.md). Non-negotiables in SKILL.md survive any brand override.

- **Register must match the subject's meaning.** Tone is read off the content first. A loud, heavy, condensed treatment applied to a quiet, contemplative subject doesn't read as bold. It reads as comical. A mismatch between voice and subject is a failure regardless of how well-crafted each part is. `L1` · R011
- **Tone moves the dials, never the skeleton.** Across registers the structure holds: the layout, reading order, image-first logic, hierarchy, accessible contrast and one text block. Tone changes the voice: the typeface, palette brightness and size, and decorative containers. A quiet subject gets an editorial serif with muted, restrained color. A playful subject gets a friendly rounded sans, brighter saturated color, more hues, and color fields behind labels and key details. Applying the quiet house style unchanged to a playful brief is wrong. `L1` (structure) · `L2` (voice) · R056
- **Playful, but disciplined, and pushed with confidence.** For playful work, go further than a timid recolor: solid color pills and badges behind labels and dates are welcome, as is a broader palette. Everything stays square to the grid, with no sticker tilts, and the headline stays one color. Playful energy comes from type, color and containers, never from breaking alignment or splitting an element's color. `L2 · playful` · R056, R057
- **Luxury: a deep jewel-toned field, a high-contrast Didone at full display scale, and metallic warmth.** A dark field drawn from the imagery (velvet plum, for example) reads as premium. A high-contrast Didone headline at a large size, white on the field, carries the luxury voice best, ahead of light tracked caps. A gold accent marks the date. The headline keeps its dominant scale. Luxury restraint applies to ornament and palette, never to hierarchy. `L2 · luxury` · R059, R060
- **No fixed default register: tone is read from the subject every time.** Across quiet, playful, energetic and luxury briefs, the choice always followed the content. Asked twice for a personal default, no answer was given, and the behavior shows why: the subject sets the register. `L1` · R011, R056–R060
- *Open question:* Anthony's default register when the brief doesn't set one has not been answered yet (asked in R011 and R012). Probe it indirectly in a later round rather than asking a third time. `TONE-01`
